paragraphs.text: An iron cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, made in 1990 and pressed hard under a [hydraulic press](sheng:pressing). Its Blue Seal Green Label designation comes from the era of state production, when pu’er was made in [state factories](sheng:history) to standard recipes and sold under the state tea company’s labels.

Pressing decides how a tea ages, and a cake this tight changes slowly. At thirty-six years it is past both the ten years some count as [aged raw pu’er](sheng:ageing) and the twenty or more that many wait for. The [slow change of storage](sheng:aging) is part of this cake’s own history.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
